lesson.title: Counting All the Regions: Electron Domain Geometry
lesson.summary: Electron geometry names the arrangement formed by every electron domain around a central atom, bonding pairs and lone pairs together, and it is the scaffold from which the visible shape of the molecule is later built.
lesson.body:
Once VSEPR theory establishes that electron domains push apart to minimize repulsion, the next question is what shape that pushing actually produces. Electron geometry answers that question by describing the spatial arrangement of every domain around the central atom, counting bonding pairs and lone pairs as equal citizens. It does not matter yet whether a given domain is an atom bonded to the center or an unshared lone pair sitting quietly nearby, both occupy a position in the geometric pattern and both are counted toward the total, called the steric number.

There are only five basic electron geometries that show up across the vast majority of main group chemistry, and each one is determined purely by the steric number. Two domains produce a linear arrangement, with the two regions on opposite sides of the central atom, 180 degrees apart. Three domains produce a trigonal planar arrangement, all three spread evenly in one flat plane, 120 degrees apart. Four domains produce a tetrahedral arrangement, spreading into three dimensions with each domain 109.5 degrees from its neighbors. Five domains produce a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement, and six domains produce an octahedral arrangement, both of which require an expanded octet on the central atom and are covered in more depth in later chapters.

A helpful example that shows why electron geometry has to be considered on its own, separate from what atoms you can actually see, is sulfur tetrafluoride, SF4. Sulfur sits at the center with four bonding pairs to four fluorine atoms and one lone pair left over, since sulfur is a period three element capable of holding more than eight electrons. Adding the four bonding domains and the one lone pair domain gives a steric number of five. The electron geometry is therefore trigonal bipyramidal, even though the visible shape traced out by the five atoms alone, called the molecular geometry, turns out to look different once the lone pair is set aside from the naming, a distinction explored fully in the next chapter.

This example highlights an important and sometimes confusing feature of electron geometry: it is always one of the five symmetric shapes for a given steric number, regardless of whether every domain is a visible bonded atom or an invisible lone pair. A lone pair still claims a position in space and still pushes on its neighbors even though there is no atom there to draw. Because of this, electron geometry is best thought of as the complete geometric skeleton of the central atom's electron cloud, the underlying framework that determines how the actual atoms will ultimately be positioned once the lone pairs are accounted for.

Getting electron geometry right is a purely mechanical exercise once the Lewis structure is correct: count every bonding pair as one domain, count every lone pair as one more domain, add them together for the steric number, then match that number to one of the five named shapes. There is no ambiguity and no judgment call involved. That reliability is exactly why electron geometry serves as such a solid foundation for predicting the molecular geometry, the shape defined only by where the atoms sit, which is the shape chemists actually draw, name, and use to reason about polarity and reactivity.
